proposals.definition: Mallārī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 30 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation transcribes the name as mal la re instead of translating it. Later Indian music knows a rāga Mallār (Malhār) sung in the rainy season; whether it is the same melody is uncertain.
proposals.rationale: Rāga names in the song headings get keep-source entries, like Paṭamañjarī and Bhairavī, and this one is not yet in the glossary.

proposals.definition: A cloud (Old Bengali meha, from Sanskrit megha; Tibetan sprin). Song 30 opens with a cloud of compassion that spreads without cease; Mahāyāna writing sometimes likens compassion to a rain cloud that waters all alike. Munidatta's gloss on the phrase speaks instead of the purified enjoyment body of the lord of yogis spreading forth by the guru's grace (cp.30.m2).
proposals.symbolicImage: a cloud of compassion that spreads without cease

symbolicReadings.referent: the purified enjoyment body (pariśuddhasambhogakāya) of the lord of yogis, which spreads forth (prasphurita) by the guru's grace once being and nonbeing, the conceptualization of the grasped and the rest, have been split and made without intrinsic nature; the gloss stands under karuṇa and does not name the cloud; the Tibetan comment agrees (longs spyod rdzogs pa'i sku ... 'phro ba)

proposals.rationale: The cloud of compassion opens the song and carries Munidatta's reading as the enjoyment body; 'cloud' renders meha plainly, and the whole-word pattern keeps it out of longer words.

proposals.definition: The enjoyment body (sambhogakāya; Tibetan longs spyod rdzogs pa'i sku): in Mahāyāna accounts of a buddha's bodies, the glorious form in which a buddha appears to bodhisattvas, between the dharma body and the emanation body. Munidatta, glossing the cloud of compassion, speaks of the purified enjoyment body of the lord of yogis spreading forth by the guru's grace (cp.30.m2).
proposals.rationale: A standard doctrinal term, new in this commentary; 'enjoyment body' is the usual English and sits beside the existing 'wheel of enjoyment' and 'body of great bliss'.

proposals.definition: A magic show or conjuring display (Sanskrit indrajāla, 'Indra's net'; Old Bengali indiāla), a stock image for what seems real and is not. In song 30 (3a) the indiāla breaks; the Tibetan line has mig 'phrul, 'magic show'. Munidatta takes the word as the host of the senses (indriyasamūha) and quotes Saraha on the senses dissolving (cp.30.m4).

symbolicReadings.referent: the host of the senses (indriyasamūha), which breaks apart and flees on beholding innate joy; he glosses indiālam as if it came from indriya, 'sense', and backs this with Saraha's line on where the senses dissolve; the Tibetan comment agrees (mig 'phrul ni dbang po'i tshogs)

proposals.rationale: The word is rare and its sense is split between the Tibetan's 'magic show' (indrajāla) and Munidatta's 'senses' (indriya); an entry fixes the rendering, which follows the likelier derivation and the Tibetan, and records his reading.

proposals.definition: A wonder or marvel (Old Bengali adabhūā, Sanskrit adbhuta; Tibetan ya mtshan): something astonishing; in Sanskrit poetics also the mood (rasa) of the marvellous. The refrain of song 30 says a wonder has risen in the middle of the sky. Munidatta's paraphrase speaks of the arising of the fruit, wondrous coupled union, in clear light (cp.30.m3).
proposals.symbolicImage: a wonder risen in the middle of the sky

symbolicReadings.referent: the arising of the fruit, wondrous coupled union (adbhutayuganaddhaphalodaya), in clear light (prabhāsvara): his paraphrase of the refrain puts clear light where the song has the middle of the sky; the Tibetan comment agrees ('od gsal ya mtshan che ba zung 'jug gi 'bras bu shar ba)

proposals.rationale: The refrain's central image, which Munidatta reads as coupled union; 'wonder' keeps the image plain and leaves the reading to a note.

proposals.definition: Darkness (Sanskrit andhakāra, Old Bengali andhakārā; Tibetan mun pa). The last line of song 30 says Bhusuku the yogin dispels it. Munidatta reads it as the darkness of the afflictions, dispelled by the rising of the fourth joy (cp.30.m6), and in the previous comment has the moon of innate joy destroy the darkness of delusion (cp.30.m5). Compare night (rajanī).
proposals.symbolicImage: the darkness that Bhusuku the yogin dispels

symbolicReadings.referent: the darkness of the afflictions (kleśāndhakāra), which the siddha master Bhusukupāda dispels by the rising of the fourth joy, apart from which there is no other means in the three worlds; the Tibetan comment agrees (nyon mongs pa'i mun pa bsal ba)
the darkness of delusion (mohāndhakāra), destroyed by the moon of innate joy (sahajānandacandra); said in his comment on couplet 4, where the song names no darkness; the Tibetan has gti mug gi mun pa

proposals.rationale: A recurring image (compare night) that Munidatta glosses here; the extra form ন্ধকার catches the word inside sandhi compounds such as kleśāndhakāra, where the initial অ disappears.

proposals.definition: Purity or purification (viśuddhi; Tibetan rnam dag): in Buddhist tantra, seeing the sense objects, aggregates and elements as pure by nature, or making them so. Song 30 (4a) speaks of the purity of the sense objects, in which the poet understood in joy; Munidatta likens it to the moon lighting up the sky (cp.30.m5).
proposals.rationale: A doctrinal term not yet in the glossary; 'purity' fits the song's 'purity of the sense objects', with 'purification' for Munidatta's process sense.

proposals.definition: Power or efficacy (prabhāva; Tibetan mthu). Munidatta uses the word to introduce couplets: in song 30 the refrain, his second verse and his fourth verse each set out 'its power' (tasya prabhāva), in cp.30.m4 the power of innate joy (cp.30.m3, cp.30.m4, cp.30.m6). Compare his other framing words, such as praise (anuśaṃsā).
proposals.rationale: A framing word Munidatta repeats three times in this comment; a single rendering keeps the woven commentary consistent, and the Tibetan pattern keeps mthu out of mthun.

proposals.definition: Duality, a pair of opposites (Old Bengali dvandala, apparently from Sanskrit dvandva, 'pair, opposition'). Song 30 (1b) speaks of splitting being and nonbeing, dvandala. Munidatta's paraphrase sets 'the conceptualization of the grasped and the rest' beside being and nonbeing in its place (cp.30.m2); the Tibetan line has no clear equivalent. The sense is uncertain.
proposals.rationale: A doctrinally loaded word of uncertain form; an entry fixes 'duality' as the rendering and flags the doubt for later songs.

proposals.definition: The fruit or result (phala; Tibetan 'bras bu) of the path, as against the path itself; in Munidatta's comments often innate joy or coupled union. He speaks of the arising of the fruit, wondrous coupled union (cp.30.m3), and introduces the last couplet of song 30 as stating the power of that joy once the fruit is attained (cp.30.m6).
proposals.rationale: A basic Buddhist term (path and fruit) that Munidatta uses to frame couplets; the pattern skips phalaka, 'board'.

proposals.definition: Bhusukupāda, the siddha to whom song 30 is ascribed; he names himself Bhusuku in its refrain and last line. Munidatta calls him Bhusukupāda and siddha master (cp.30.m1, cp.30.m6) and has him address himself (cp.30.m3).
proposals.rationale: Adds the nominative and the vocative (bho bhusukupāda) of this commentary to the existing entry.

proposals.definition: The pair being and nonbeing (bhāva, abhāva). Song 30 (1b) speaks of splitting them; Munidatta repeats bhāvābhāva and sets the conceptualization of the grasped and the rest beside it (cp.30.m2).
proposals.rationale: Adds Munidatta's Sanskrit form and the Tibetan line's wording, which the existing Tibetan forms do not match.

proposals.definition: True nature (Old Bengali saruā, Sanskrit svarūpa). The refrain of song 30 tells Bhusuku to look at the innate true nature; Munidatta has 'the true nature of innate joy' (sahajānandasvarūpa) (cp.30.m3).
proposals.rationale: A new spelling (saruā) of the Old Bengali word, which the existing form সরুঅ does not match.

proposals.definition: The senses (indriya). Munidatta glosses the song's indiāla as the host of the senses (indriyasamūha) and quotes Saraha's Apabhraṃśa line india jathu vilīa gau, 'where the senses dissolved' (cp.30.m4).
proposals.rationale: Adds the Apabhraṃśa form india from the Saraha quotation and Munidatta's indriyasamūha; ইন্দিঅ does not occur inside ইন্দিআল.

proposals.definition: Mind. Song 30 (3b) speaks of one's own mind (ṇia mana, Sanskrit manas); Munidatta renders it nijamanaḥ and equates it with bodhicitta (cp.30.m4). The Tibetan has yid, as the entry already records.
proposals.rationale: Adds Old Bengali mana and Sanskrit manas under the existing "mind" entry, with whole-word patterns because মন sits inside many unrelated words.

proposals.definition: The objects of the senses. Song 30 (4a) speaks of their purity (bisaa biśuddhim̐); Munidatta has viṣayāṇāṃ viśuddhyā (cp.30.m5), and the Tibetan yul.
proposals.rationale: A new Old Bengali spelling (bisaa) that the existing form বিষয় does not match.

proposals.definition: Joy. In song 30 (4a) the poet understood 'in joy'; Munidatta explains it as supreme joy understood in the joy of cessation (cp.30.m5), and speaks of seeing the true nature of innate joy in the third joy (cp.30.m3).
proposals.rationale: Adds the first Old Bengali form of the word and the third joy (tṛtīyānanda) of this commentary.

proposals.definition: Sky. Song 30 has a wonder rise in the middle of the sky (2a) and the moon light up the sky (4b, genitive gaaṇaha).
proposals.rationale: Adds the genitive gaaṇaha of line 4b.

proposals.definition: The moon, which in song 30 (4b) lights up the sky; Munidatta repeats the simile and speaks of the moon of innate joy (cp.30.m5).
proposals.rationale: Adds the inflected forms cānde and candreṇa attested in this song.

proposals.definition: The three worlds. Song 30 (5a) has the Old Bengali locative tailoe, which Munidatta cites as eteloe and renders etasmin trailo(ka), 'in this threefold world' (cp.30.m6); the Tibetan has khams gsum and 'jig rten gsum.
proposals.rationale: Adds the Old Bengali tailoe, Munidatta's citation of it, and the restored trailo(ka), which the existing forms do not match.

proposals.definition: Clear light. Munidatta says the fruit, wondrous coupled union, arose in clear light (cp.30.m3); the manuscript folio number falls inside the word.
proposals.rationale: The folio number [45ka] splits the word in the source, so the plain form would miss it; this records the attested spelling.

proposals.definition: Supreme joy, the second of the four joys. Munidatta speaks of understanding it in the joy of cessation (cp.30.m5); the Tibetan has the short form mchog dga'.
proposals.rationale: Adds the short Tibetan form mchog dga', which the existing mchog tu dga' ba does not match.

proposals.definition: Praise or commendation. Munidatta introduces his third verse of song 30 as stating 'the praise of the path' (mārgasyānuśaṃsā) (cp.30.m5); the Tibetan has lam gyi rjes su bsngags pa.
proposals.rationale: Adds the form of this commentary; the match form catches anuśaṃsām after any sandhi vowel.

questions: Readings for existing entries that a forms-only proposal cannot carry, for the reviewer to add if wanted: moon → the moon of innate joy (sahajānandacandra), which destroys the darkness of delusion (cp.30.m5); sky → clear light, since Munidatta's paraphrase of the refrain has prabhāsvare where the song has gaaṇa mājhem̐, 'in the middle of the sky' (cp.30.m3); mind → one's own mind (ṇia mana) as bodhicitta (nijamanaḥ bodhicittaṃ, cp.30.m4); joy (4a ānande) → supreme joy understood in the joy of cessation (cp.30.m5).

indiāla (3a): I propose 'magic show' (indrajāla, as the Tibetan line's mig 'phrul reads it) and treat Munidatta's 'host of the senses' (indriyasamūha, cp.30.m4) as his reading, so 'senses' is listed as forbidden in the line. If you take the literal sense to be 'senses' (from indriya), drop the forbidden list and change the rendering.

I added Old Bengali mana and Sanskrit (nija)manaḥ to the existing citta entry ('mind'), which already lists Tibetan yid, rather than opening a separate manas entry. Say if you would prefer a separate entry. The patterns are whole-word because মন sits inside many unrelated words.

cp.30.m3: Shastri restores ataev[ā]gamaḥ, which reads as āgama, 'scripture', but the Tibetan has de las de kho na nyid rtogs pa, suggesting avagamaḥ, 'understanding'. This word should probably not be tagged with the agama ('scripture') entry.

cp.30.3b: the Bengali reads ṇia mana ṇa de ulāsa, with a negative ṇa, but Munidatta (sahajollāsaṃ dadāti) and the Tibetan line (rang gi yid la dga' ba ster bar byed) both say the mind gives delight, with no negative. This is not a glossary point, but the line drafter should flag it.

dvandala (1b): the form and sense are uncertain. 'Duality' assumes Sanskrit dvandva. The Tibetan line (dngos po dngos med rtog cing rtog cing sel) has no clear equivalent, and Munidatta puts 'the conceptualization of the grasped and the rest' in its place.

megha: Munidatta's enjoyment-body gloss (cp.30.m2) stands under karuṇa, not under the cloud. I recorded it on the cloud entry because the gloss covers the whole image 'cloud of compassion'. You may want it noted under compassion (karuna) as well.
